questions.q: Someone in England earns {s} a year, with no pension or student loan. How much income tax do they pay in the year?
questions.why: Tax-free up to £12,570, then 20% on the rest: 20% × ({s} − £12,570) = {answer}.

questions.q: An employee earns {s} a year. How much employee National Insurance do they pay in the year?
In England, someone earns {s} a year, with no pension or student loan. Roughly what's their take-home pay each month? (Within £5.)
What does the tax code 1257L tell your employer?
options: You can earn £12,570 a year tax-free
You have paid £1,257 in tax so far
questions.why: 1257 → £12,570 of tax-free pay; L is the standard Personal Allowance. Scottish codes start with S.

questions.q: If a pay rise takes you into the 40% band, all of your pay is then taxed at 40%.
questions.why: Only the pay above £50,270 is taxed at 40%. Each band only taxes the slice of pay inside it.

questions.q: You earn exactly £50,270 in England and get a {r} pay rise. After 40% income tax and 2% National Insurance on the rise, how much of it do you keep?
questions.why: Only the rise is above £50,270, so you lose 40% + 2% = 42% of it and keep 58%: {answer}.

questions.q: You earn £1,800 from tutoring in 2026/27, with almost no costs. What do you need to do?
options: Register for Self Assessment by 5 October 2027 and declare it
Nothing, as long as you also have a job
Pay 20% of it to HMRC straight away
questions.why: Trading income over the £1,000 trading allowance means registering for Self Assessment by 5 October after the tax year ends.

questions.q: Put the Self Assessment steps for a new side hustle in order, first to last.
items: Earn over £1,000 from trading in the tax year
The tax year ends on 5 April
Register for Self Assessment by 5 October
File your return and pay by 31 January
questions.why: Go over £1,000, wait for the tax year to end, register by 5 October, then file and pay by 31 January.

questions.q: Match each payslip word to what it means.
pairs: Your employer takes tax off for you
questions.why: Gross minus deductions (tax, NI, pension, loan) gives net. PAYE is how employers collect tax; NI years count towards the State Pension.

questions.q: Which of these is different if you live in Scotland?
options: Income tax bands and rates on wages
Whether you get a Personal Allowance
questions.why: Scotland sets its own income tax bands on wages (six of them). NI, the Personal Allowance and PAYE work the same across the UK.

questions.q: A friend turns down a pay rise because it would "put them in a higher tax band". Explain why that's a mistake.

ideas.label: Only the extra pay above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate
The rest of their pay keeps its old rate, so they still take home more

questions.model: Only the pay above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate. Everything below it keeps its old rate, so they still take home more than before: on a £1,000 rise over £50,270 they'd keep £580.
questions.why: Tax bands are slices, not a switch for your whole pay.

tests.answer: Only the slice of pay above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate; the rest stays at the same rate, so they still take home more.
Only the extra money gets taxed more.
Because tax is lower when you earn more.

questions.q: Your Saturday job pays £60 a week, all year. Explain why no income tax is taken off.

ideas.label: It's under the Personal Allowance (tax-free amount)
The allowance is yearly, and the job pays only about £3,120 over a year

questions.model: £60 × 52 is about £3,120 a year. The Personal Allowance is £12,570 a year, so all of it is tax-free (and it's under the National Insurance threshold too).
questions.why: Allowances are yearly, so small part-time jobs usually pay no income tax.

tests.answer: Over a year that's about £3,120, which is under the £12,570 personal allowance.
